questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman presented to the clinic for a follow-up visit after receiving a diagnosis of pulmonary histoplasmosis. Two weeks prior, the patient had presented to the clinic with cough and fevers and received a diagnosis of pulmonary histoplasmosis. At this follow-up visit, the patient reported an improvement in the cough and resolution of fevers. The patient had no known drug allergies. The patient’s comorbidities included hypertension and diabetes. Medications included the following: Itraconazole 10 mg/mL oral solution – take 20 mL by mouth twice daily (started 2 weeks ago) Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg by mouth once daily Aspirin 81 mg by mouth once daily Metformin 500 mg by mouth twice daily Atorvastatin 10 mg by mouth once daily Omeprazole 20 mg by mouth once daily The patient denied any missed doses of medications and reported taking the itraconazole solution on an empty stomach. Investigations: Serum itraconazole 0.8 μg/mL Serum hydroxyitraconazole 1.5 μg/mL Creatinine 1 mg/dL ALT 15 U/L
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Change to itraconazole capsules 200 mg by mouth twice daily
Change to posaconazole DR tabs 100 mg – take 3 tablets by mouth once daily
Continue itraconazole oral solution 200 mg by mouth twice daily
Educate the patient to take the itraconazole solution with food and repeat itraconazole serum concentration in 2 weeks
Increase itraconazole oral solution to 400 mg by mouth twice daily

questions.explanation: Continue itraconazole oral solution 200 mg by mouth twice daily The patient started the itraconazole 2 weeks ago and reported 100% adherence. The itraconazole was at steady state, and the timing of the blood draw in relation to the timing of administration will not make a clinically significant difference. The patient’s itraconazole level was the sum of the itraconazole (0.8 μg/mL) and hydroxyitraconazole (1.5 μg/mL). A level of 2.1 μg/mL is between the goal range of 1–10 μg/mL. Continuing the same formulation and dose is most appropriate. The dose does not need to be increased, and doses above 200 mg are best split into multiple doses to maximize absorption. The patient is correctly taking itraconazole solution on an empty stomach to maximize absorption, and the patient should not be advised to take itraconazole with food. Itraconazole solution has better bioavailability than the capsule formulation, and the capsule formulation absorption will be inhibited by the omeprazole. The patient has shown clinical improvement, a therapeutic itraconazole level, and no adverse drug reactions secondary to itraconazole. There is no need to change to another agent with relatively less data and experience.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q7

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man presented with fever, productive cough, lethargy, weakness, and malaise. He was known to have HIV but was not taking ART . He lived in Missouri. His respiratory status and mental status deteriorated, and he was transferred to the ICU. Investigations: HIV viral load 174,000 copies/mL CD4 count 1 cell/μL CXR: atelectasis and superimposed pneumonia BAL: routine bacterial, fungal, and AFB cultures negative BAL: PCR for adenovirus, CMV , and HSV negative Pneumocystis DFA on BAL and induced sputum negative Respiratory viral panel negative Legionella urine antigen and Legionella antibody negative Serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen negative Histoplasma urine antigen negative Antibodies for Blastomyces, Coccidioides, and West Nile virus negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate additional test to request?

options.text: West Nile virus antibody on CSF

questions.explanation: Legionella culture on BAL The Legionella urine antigen test only detects L. pneumophila serogroup 1. Although L. pneumophila serogroup 1 is the most common cause of infection and the urine antigen test has a fast turnaround time, a negative urine antigen does not effectively rule out Legionella. Culture and some PCRs detect all species of Legionella and should be ordered in addition to the urine antigen. BAL is not an appropriate specimen for anaerobic culture, and an anaerobic infection is low on the differential. If anaerobic cultures were desired, a bronchial brushing or lung biopsy should be performed. C. psittaci does not fit since there is no bird exposure. It is diagnosed by serology rather than PCR/NAAT . Serology is not the preferred test for diagnosis of M. pneumoniae. The correct test would be PCR/NAAT . WNV antibodies are not found in CSF without also being found in serum. Since the serum serology was negative, the CSF serology will also be negative.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q2

questions.stem: A 30-year-old patient was diagnosed with disseminated histoplasmosis. The patient was known to have HIV , well controlled on cobicistat/darunavir 150/800 mg and tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine 25/200 mg by mouth once daily. The patient did not take any other medications. Kidney and liver function were normal. The patient weighed 60 kg and had no known allergies.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication regimen for empiric maintenance therapy for disseminated histoplasmosis?

options.text: Itraconazole capsules 200 mg by mouth twice daily
Itraconazole capsules 400 mg by mouth once daily
Itraconazole oral solution 200 mg by mouth once daily
Itraconazole oral solution 200 mg by mouth twice daily
Liposomal amphotericin B 300 mg IV once daily

questions.explanation: Itraconazole oral solution 200 mg by mouth once daily Itraconazole is the recommended treatment of disseminated histoplasmosis during the maintenance phase of therapy. The itraconazole oral solution formulation is preferred over the capsule formulation due to increased bioavailability. Itraconazole doses greater than 200 mg should be split into multiple doses to help optimize absorption. Itraconazole is a major substrate of CYP450 3A4. Cobicistat/darunavir is a strong CYP450 3A4 inhibitor, which will decrease the metabolism of itraconazole, resulting in increased itraconazole levels. Itraconazole inhibits the metabolism of cobicistat/darunavir, resulting in an increase in darunavir. The interaction is clinically significant. The usual, i.e., in the setting of no drug–drug interactions, itraconazole maintenance dose is 200 mg by mouth twice daily. With these drug–drug interactions in place, the recommendation is to reduce the itraconazole dose to 200 mg once daily, and then check itraconazole levels.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q6

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presented with fever, night sweats, dry cough, diarrhea, and 30 pound weight loss in 2 months. He lived in Indianapolis, IN. On exam he was febrile to 38.3°C, had oral thrush, nontender cervical and axillary adenopathy, a palpable spleen tip, and a diffuse papular rash. Investigations: Total white cell count 2 ×109/L Hemoglobin 80 g/L Platelets 75 ×109/L AST 163 U/L ALT 80 U/L Alkaline phosphatase 400 U/L CXR: bilateral reticulonodular infiltrates HIV Ag/Ab positive Absolute CD4 count 55 cells/μL Blood cultures: blood smear shown below
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Histoplasma capsulatum The presence of fever and a chronic wasting illness associated with adenopathy, splenomegaly, pancytopenia, mild transaminitis, and reticulonodular infiltrates suggests an opportunistic infection in the setting of advanced HIV infection. While HIV itself could account for some of the symptoms and findings, fever, reticulonodular infiltrates (miliary pattern), and splenomegaly support a concomitant infection. Blood cultures grew yeast and peripheral smear shows small intracellular organisms. The yeast do not have the appearance of Cryptococcus, which is a large round cell with a surrounding capsule. Given that the patient lives in an endemic region, the likeliest diagnosis is disseminated histoplasmosis associated with advanced HIV infection. (Image from Bibbo M, Wilbur DC. Comprehensive Cytopathology. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2015.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q29

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presented with neutropenic fevers and headache. He had finished induction therapy with cytarabine and daunorubicin 3 weeks ago after a new diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia. B A He had no other significant past medical history. He was a nonsmoker and only drank alcohol occasionally. He worked for a local chicken farm in Missouri. On examination, his temperature was 39.8°C, his heart rate was 110 beats/minute, blood pressure 80/58 mmHg, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/minute with SPO2 95% on 2L. There was redness and tenderness over right subclavian Hohn catheter site. Lung exam showed decreased breath sounds on bilateral bases with scattered crackles. The Hohn catheter was removed, and he was started on vancomycin and cefepime. Investigations: Absolute neutrophil count 300 cells/μL CXR: bibasilar scarring with no obvious consolidation CT head: bilateral mild maxillary sinusitis Blood cultures and catheter tip cultures: yeast Serum galactomannan-negative Serum cryptococcal antigen-positive with a titer of 1:64
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely etiologic agent?
questions.explanation: Trichosporon sp. Neutropenic fevers in immunocompromised patients have broad differential, including bacterial as well fungal etiologies. Line-associated sepsis with blood culture positive for yeast could represent Candida, Rhodotorula, Trichosporon, or Cryptococcus. Pseudohyphae with barrel-shaped arthroconidia and pleomorphic budding yeast favors Candida or Trichosporon. Cryptococcus are round yeast with no budding or pseudohyphae. The positive cryptococcal antigen is likely to be a falsepositive (Cryptococcus sp. would grow as a yeast) and raises the concern for infection with Trichosporon. Management includes line removal and antifungal with amphotericin or voriconazole. (Image from Lee W-S, Yu F-L, Ou T-Y. Breakthrough Trichosporon asahii fungemia during caspofungin therapy. J Exp Clin Med. 2014;6(3):108–109.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q2

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man with HIV was admitted to the hospital with septic shock. His CD4 count was 25/ μL, and he was not on antiretroviral therapy. On examination, he had diffuse rhonchi, and he was noted to have multiple papular skin lesions. His chest radiograph showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. He was started on broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy. Four days into his hospitalization, his blood cultures grew mold. He also had a skin biopsy done and Gomori methenamine stain of the tissue shows 2–4 μm yeast forms (see image).
questions.lead_in: In addition to antibacterial therapy, what other antimicrobials should be instituted?
questions.explanation: Amphotericin B This patient has disseminated histoplasmosis, which can cause a sepsis syndrome in patients with HIV . He should receive amphotericin. Caution should also be taken to look for additional opportunistic processes as with his degree of immunocompromise he is at risk of having more than one disease process. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q33

questions.lead_in: The yeast seen in this lung biopsy specimen is most likely what organism?
questions.explanation: Coccidioides immitis This specimen shows several Coccidioides spherules containing endospores. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q34

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman presented with 1 week of fevers, chills, abdominal pain, and lethargy. She was known to have advanced HIV disease on antiretroviral therapy. She also had a history of diabetes, hypertension, mild chronic kidney disease, and transient ischemic attacks. The patient lived in Dallas, Texas, and worked as a secretary at a construction job site. On examination, her blood pressure was 85/55mmHg and her heart rate was 130 beats/minute. Pulmonary exam was normal, but there was diffuse abdominal tenderness with hepatomegaly but no peritonitis. Investigations: CD4 count 65 cells/μL HIV viral load 235 copies/mL Lactate dehydrogenase 865 U/L (122–222) Ferritin 1550 ng/mL (20–200) Peripheral blood smear:
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Histoplasma capsulatum The patient’s clinical presentation is most consistent with progressive disseminated histoplasmosis caused by Histoplasma capsulatum seen in advanced HIV disease. This endemic fungi is seen in the Ohio and Mississippi river valley extending down into the South as far as Texas. Typical presentations include fevers, hepatosplenomegaly, and multiorgan involvement that can progress to septic shock. Marked elevations in LDH and ferritin can be seen although these are nonspecific. The peripheral blood smear may show characteristic intracellular, 2–4 μm yeast forms in the WBCs, as seen in the image. The geographic epidemiology, clinical presentation and peripheral smear findings are not compatible with the other endemic fungi listed. (Image from Singh NK, Nagendra S. Histoplasma capsulatum peripheral blood smear. BMJ Case Reports. https://d oi.org/10.1136/bcr.05.2009.1877.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q21

questions.lead_in: The yeast seen in this lymph node aspirate is most likely what organism?
questions.explanation: Paracoccidioides brasiliensis This image shows the typical “pilot’s wheel” appearance of Paracoccidioides. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q34

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of fevers, cough, and pleuritic chest pain. The symptoms were gradually progressive and accompanied by night sweats and a 15 lb weight loss. She was known to have HIV but was not taking ART . She worked as a horse trainer in Kentucky and 6 months earlier had spent a 2-week vacation in Kenya. On examination she was cachectic and right upper lobe rales were audible on pulmonary examination. Investigations: CD4 count 26 cells/μL HIV viral load 25,600 copies/mL Sputum microscopy: neutrophils and abundant grampositive coccobacilli seen Sputum culture: salmon-pink mucoid colonies seen that revealed gram-positive branching filamentous rods Sputum AFB stains positive but Mycobacterium tuberculosis and M. avium-intracellulare PCR on sputum and cultures were negative CXR: 2 cm right upper lobe cavitary lung lesion
questions.lead_in: What pathogen is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Rhodococcus equi An unusual opportunistic infection that can cause cavitary pulmonary disease in advanced HIV disease is Rhodococcus equi. This pathogen is a gram-positive coccobacillus or diphtheroids on Gram stain but can be seen as branching rods from liquid media. It can also be AFB-positive on stains, but the negative MTB and MAI PCRs make these pathogens much less likely. There is an association of this pathogen with exposure to horses and other livestock although only about 50% of patients recall this specific exposure history.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q23

parts.text: Give two reasons for a positive India ink with a negative cryptococcal antigen test.

parts_raw.text: What are 2 reasons for the scenario: Positive India Ink / Negative cryptococcal antigen test
What are 2 reasons for the scenario: Negative India Ink / Positive cryptococcal antigen test
What antifungal should you not use and give 2 reasons why.
In 5 days, the lab is growing a white mycelia on culture. 2 possibilities?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Misinterpretation of the smear - lymphocytes with surrounding proteinaceous debris mistaken for encapsulated yeast (India ink requires experience); (2) an encapsulated organism whose capsule lacks the glucuronoxylomannan detected by CrAg (a non-neoformans/non-gattii Cryptococcus or Trichosporon) - or a prozone/high-titre effect on the antigen assay. b) (1) Low organism burden - India ink is only ~50% sensitive in non-AIDS meningitis, so few yeasts are missed on microscopy; (2) early/low-count meningitis in which antigen is detectable before enough yeast are present to be seen or cultured. c) Do not use an echinocandin (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin): (1) it has no reliable anticryptococcal activity; (2) Cryptococcus has high MICs to echinocandins in vitro. d) (1) Cryptococcus itself producing hyphal/pseudohyphal structures under stress/mating conditions in vitro; (2) a separate mould - an environmental contaminant or an endemic dimorphic fungus in mould phase acquired during US travel (e.g., Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides).
questions.beyond_mandell: The identity of the specific dimorphic mould given US travel (Histoplasma/Blastomyces/Coccidioides) rests on endemic-mycosis knowledge, not this chapter.

parts.text: What infection control measures are needed for the nurse?
What infection control measures are needed for the lab technician?
Given what you know about the life cycle, how could it be acquired?
What are two indications to treat?

parts_raw.text: Infection control measures for nurse?
Infection control measures for lab technician.
Given what you know about the life cycle how could it be acquired?
What are 2-indications to treat?

questions.model_answer: a) Routine/standard precautions – no person-to-person transmission. b) Biosafety Level 2 practices suffice for handling yeast-phase clinical specimens; Biosafety Level 3 is required when propagating the sporulating mould phase or processing soil, with mould-phase work done in a biological safety cabinet. c) By inhalation of microconidia aerosolized from bird/bat guano-enriched soil that has been disturbed, or from sporulating mould cultures in the laboratory. d) (1) Immunosuppression (transplant recipient), at risk of progressive disseminated disease. (2) Failure to improve after >1 month of illness or hypoxemia.
questions.beyond_mandell: BSL-2 for yeast-phase specimen handling reflects standard laboratory biosafety guidance; Mandell text explicitly states only that mycelial-phase manipulation requires BSL-3. Immunosuppression as a treatment indication is IDSA-based.

cohort_answer.text: Nurse: Routine practices. Lab technician: Laboratory Safety and Containment - infective stage (conidia) present in sporulating mold form cultures and soil from endemic areas; yeast form in tissues/fluids may cause local infection via parenteral inoculation or mucous membrane splash; BSL-2/ABSL-2 practices recommended for handling/processing clinical specimens, identifying isolates, animal tissues, mold cultures (any culture identifying dimorphic fungi handled in Class II BSC); BSL-3 practices for propagating sporulating cultures in mold form or processing soil/environmental materials likely to contain infectious conidia. Summary: BSL2 minimum for yeast-form specimens, BSL3 when propagating spores in mold/soil. Acquisition: grows in soil enriched with guano from avian species/bats; spores circulate in air after soil disturbed; acquired through inhalation of spores; once inhaled, converts to yeast form due to body temp, activates inflammatory cascade, travels to lymph nodes to spread. Indications to treat: acute pulmonary histo if symptoms not better after >1 month of illness or hypoxemia (most people with acute pulm histo don't need therapy, just bed rest+antipyretics); cavitary pulmonary histo (progressive loss of pulmonary function without treatment); acute disseminated histo; histo-related meningitis and endocarditis. Do not need to treat: pericarditis, arthropathies (treat with NSAIDs +/- steroids); hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy from acute pulmonary histo (treat if persistent). Definite indications (proven/probable efficacy): acute diffuse pulmonary infection moderate-severe symptoms; chronic cavitary pulmonary infection; progressive disseminated infection; CNS infection. Uncertain indication: acute focal pulmonary infection, asymptomatic or mild symptoms persisting >1 month; mediastinal lymphadenitis; mediastinal granuloma; inflammatory syndromes treated with corticosteroids. Not recommended: mediastinal fibrosis; pulmonary nodule; broncholithiasis; presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome.

questions.question: A patient develops pulmonary symptoms; cultures reveal mold growing at 30 degrees C and yeast growing at 37 degrees C. The individual has never travelled to the southwestern USA.
questions.question_raw: Q15 (2010 AM). Scenario about patient who develops pulmonary symptoms, cultures reveal mold growing at 30C and yeast growing at 37C. Told that individual has never travelled to SW USA

parts.text: Name 2 possible organisms.

parts_raw.text: A) Name 2 possible organisms

questions.model_answer: (1) Blastomyces dermatitidis; (2) Histoplasma capsulatum. Both are thermally dimorphic fungi (mould at 22-30 C, yeast at 37 C). Coccidioides is excluded by the absence of southwestern US exposure, and Paracoccidioides/Talaromyces are geographically inconsistent.

cohort_answer.text: Histoplasmosis; Blastomycosis. Dimorphic fungi grow as yeast in host, mold at room temperature in vitro; includes histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, sporotrichosis, coccidioidomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, chromoblastomycosis, adiaspiromycosis, and new Emmonsia/Emergomyces/Talaromyces agents. Mnemonic: 'Mold in the Cold, Yeast in the Heat'.

questions.model_answer: a) Routine/standard precautions only – human-to-human transmission of Histoplasma via the pulmonary route has not been reported, so no isolation is required. b) Laboratory biosafety: clinical specimens can be handled with routine practices, but manipulation/propagation of the mycelial (mould) phase is a biohazard and requires Biosafety Level 3 precautions with work in a biological safety cabinet. c) Histoplasma polysaccharide antigen detection in urine and/or serum by EIA (positive in ~70-80% of moderate-severe acute pulmonary disease); H and M precipitin bands and complement-fixation serology are complementary. d) (1) Immunosuppression (transplant recipient) – places him at high risk of progressive disseminated disease. (2) Illness that has not improved after >1 month (his symptoms have persisted ~2 months) or presence of hypoxemia.
questions.beyond_mandell: Immunosuppression as a stand-alone indication to treat acute pulmonary histoplasmosis is emphasized in the IDSA 2007 histoplasmosis guideline; Mandell text explicitly grounds only the '>1 month without improvement or hypoxemia' criterion.

cohort_answer.text: Nurse: Standard precautions. Lab tech: Containment level 3 facility as per PHAC, work under biologic safety cabinet with PPE (e.g. gloves). Other diagnostic test: Histoplasma serum + urinary antigen, serology. Transmission to HCW: If there is construction around the hospital; In lab: Inhalation of conidia spores or accidental parenteral inoculation causing cutaneous infection. Indications to initiate therapy: Bilateral involvement; Immunocompromised; Symptoms >1mo. Tx: AmphoB x1-2 weeks, followed by Itraconazole x12 weeks total.

What precautions are needed for the lab worker?
Given the life cycle, how could a healthcare worker become infected?
What are two indications for treatment in this patient?

parts_raw.text: Precautions needed for HCW, assuming correct diagnosis (1)
Precautions for lab worker (1)
Given the life cycle, how could a HCW become infected (1)
Two indications for treatment in this patient (2)

questions.model_answer: a) Routine/standard precautions – no person-to-person transmission. b) Biosafety Level 3 for propagating/manipulating the sporulating mould (mycelial) phase; use a biological safety cabinet when opening plates or performing aerosol-generating procedures. c) By inhalation of microconidia – from disturbed guano-enriched soil in the environment, or from sporulating mould cultures in the lab (the same inhalational route as the patient). d) (1) Immunosuppression (transplant recipient). (2) Symptoms persisting/not improving after >1 month (or hypoxemia).
questions.beyond_mandell: The immunosuppression treatment indication is per IDSA guidance; Mandell text grounds the '>1 month/hypoxemia' criterion directly.

cohort_answer.text: HCW precautions: Standard precautions (no person to person transmission). Lab worker: Biosafety level 3, use safety cabinet when opening plates or for aerosolizing procedures (CL3 organism must go to appropriate lab). HCW infection route: inhaling fungal spores in the environment or micro lab (same way patient did). Treatment indications: Immunocompromised; symptoms >1 month; Cavitary Pulmonary Histo, Progressive Disseminated Histo, Meningitis, Endocarditis.

questions.question: Pictures of respiratory specimens are shown. Identify the organisms in the histopathology images of respiratory fungal pathogens.
questions.question_raw: Q19 (2014). Pictures of respiratory specimens, and asked to identify: [image-based question: histopathology images of respiratory fungal pathogens]

parts.text: Identify the organisms shown in the histopathology images.

parts_raw.text: Identify the organisms shown in the histopathology images

questions.model_answer: Distinguish by tissue morphology (Table 255.2): (1) Coccidioides posadasii/immitis — 5-60 um thick-walled, nonbudding round spherules containing endospores; cavities may contain hyphae. (2) Blastomyces dermatitidis — 8-15 um round multinucleated yeast with broad-based bud (large pore, daughter attached until nearly mother's size); pyogenic and granulomatous inflammation. (3) Aspergillus spp. — 2-5 um-wide, frequently septate hyphae of even diameter with acute-angle Y-shaped branching; vascular invasion and necrosis. (4) Pneumocystis jirovecii — 3.5-7 um nonbudding cysts staining black on GMS (may show central black dot), white on calcofluor, in clusters within alveoli surrounded by eosinophilic amorphous material. (5) Talaromyces marneffei — 2-3 x 2-6 um oblong intracellular yeasts, some with a central cross-septum (division by fission, not budding).

cohort_answer.text: Coccidioides immitis: necrotizing/suppurative granulomatous inflammation, large (20-200 micron) thick-walled spherules with basophilic endospores (2-4 microns), eosinophilic infiltrate common, occasional thin septate hyphae with arthroconidia (esp diabetics). Talaromyces marneffei: (formerly Penicillium marneffei) - endemic to SE Asia/southern China/eastern India, usually with immunodeficiency; intracytoplasmic organisms similar to histoplasma, sausage cells with light blue cytoplasm and central cross walls (fission not budding), 1-2 purple-red nuclei. Blastomyces dermatitidis: mixed acute/granulomatous inflammation, large budding yeasts (8-15 micron) with broad-based buds and refractile walls, easily seen on H&E. Aspergillosis: dichotomous branching (45 degree angle) septate hyphae, 2.5-4.5 micron diameter, may see fruiting body, often invades vessels. Pneumocystis jirovecii: alveolar spaces filled with pink foamy amorphous material (proliferating fungi and debris), 4-6 micron cup/boat shaped cysts, mild inflammatory reaction with fibrin exudate/hyaline membranes; can rarely cause necrotizing granulomas/miliary disease.

questions.question: A transplant patient develops infection with histoplasmosis.
questions.question_raw: A transplant patient develops an infection with histoplasmosis.

parts.text: What are four immune phenomena you can get from histoplasmosis?
What are two other syndromes/infections with histoplasmosis?

parts_raw.text: What are 4 immune phenomenon you can get from histoplasmosis?
What are 2 other syndromes/infections with histoplasmosis?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Arthralgias/arthritis. (2) Erythema nodosum. (3) Erythema multiforme. (4) Pericarditis (inflammatory, from adjacent mediastinal nodes rather than direct invasion). Mediastinal granuloma/fibrosis is a further immune-mediated phenomenon. b) (1) Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (with hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, mucosal ulcers, CNS/adrenal involvement). (2) Chronic cavitary pulmonary histoplasmosis; other syndromes include mediastinal fibrosis, endocarditis/endovascular infection and CNS (chronic meningitis) disease.

cohort_answer.text: Immune phenomena: Pericarditis, arthritis, erythema nodosum, erythema multiforme (rarely Histo actually cultured from pericardial/joint fluid, thought inflammatory rather than infected; note adrenal insufficiency in histo is actual tissue infection, not immunologic). Other syndromes: Chronic meningitis, chronic cutaneous, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, endocarditis presentations.
